rv.q: Tim Crouch puts another batch of guest stars through the emotional wringer of this theatrical experiment in empathy and vulnerability
A solid work of experimental theatre, it’s worth seeing.
If you get lucky, you are in for an absolute treat.
As with the Michael Craig-Martin artwork it references, I can admire the concept and the artistry of the piece, while not entirely connecting to it on an emotional level.

Tim Crouch's theatrical experiment still holds weight, and that even the sceptics among us (me) can appreciate the way form and structure are played with, twisted, and occasionally abandoned altogether.
I urge you to go and experience this for yourselves.
An unusual, funny, and surprisingly moving production that's well worth experiencing.
It's alive and breathing but I'm not sure on where the journey really took me and placed me at the end.

By the end of the show the contrived avant-garde novelty of An Oak Tree had begun to wear off, and it all began to feel like a slightly pretentious and over-indulgent tutorial exercise between two theatre luvvies.
It is a tender, funny and thoughtful piece of theatre, and a reminder of how powerful live performance can be when it takes a risk.
Brave, unpredictable and at times moving, it is a fascinating watch.
The more fascinating the theatrical experiment becomes, the harder it is to engage with the human story at its centre.
Yet while I respected An Oak Tree, I rarely felt emotionally invested in it.

cn.t: Critics praise Tim Crouch's experimental two-hander as a powerful, fascinating theatrical experience that remains revelatory two decades on. The unique format—featuring a different unprepared guest actor each night—creates moving explorations of grief and performance.
